1072.title: Mental factors
1072.hook: fifty-two factors that color each moment of consciousness
1072.howItsDone: Students of the Abhidhamma in Theravada communities learn the mental factors as named lists, often from the Abhidhammattha Sangaha, and some meditation teachers use the same names to help students note what is present in the mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, four families of mind: wholesome, unwholesome, resultant and functional. Your line: four families.

A white shirt goes into the wash with one red sock and comes out pink. Same water. Same shirt. One small thing in the load, and everything has a new color. The Abhidhamma looks at a moment of mind in a similar way. In every moment there is a knowing, the plain fact of being aware of something. And riding along with that knowing are things that tint it: interest, worry, kindness, hurry, ease.
screen: `ONE RED SOCK.` → `A KNOWING.` → `AND WHAT TINTS IT.`

segments.voice: The Pali word is cetasika, a mental factor. A few days ago this path met citta, consciousness, the bare knowing that arises and passes moment by moment. A citta never comes alone. The Abhidhammattha Sangaha, a manual of the Abhidhamma, describes a mental factor this way: it arises together with consciousness, ceases together with it, takes the same object, and rests on the same base. Partners, not visitors who wander in on their own schedule. The same manual counts fifty-two of them, but the picture matters more than the number. One moment of seeing a friend's face is seeing plus recognition, plus warmth, plus maybe a small reminder that a call is overdue. The seeing is the citta. What flavors it is cetasika. The suttas have their own picture. In the Simile of the Cloth, the Buddha describes a cloth that is stained and dirty. Dip it in any dye, blue or yellow or red, and the color takes badly. Dip a clean cloth, and the color comes out clear. In the same way, he says, when the mind is stained, an unhappy destination can be expected, and when it is clean, a happy one. The stains he names there include greed, ill will, anger, envy and conceit. The Abhidhamma sorts lists like that carefully: which factors stain, which brighten, and which are present no matter what. Here's why that's useful. A mood, seen this way, is a factor in a moment, one dye among several. It arrived, and it can pass. Over the next days come the families: the factors in every moment, the troubled ones, and the beautiful ones.
screen: `A CITTA NEVER COMES ALONE.` · `PARTNERS, NOT VISITORS.` · `A STAINED CLOTH TAKES DYE BADLY.` · then, large: `A MOOD IS A FACTOR IN A MOMENT.`

segments.voice: If you'd like, look at this moment the way a dyer looks at cloth: there is knowing, a sound, the seat, the breath, and there is its color. Name three colors quietly in plain words, like tired, curious, a little restless, without fixing any of them. Each one is a color on the knowing, not the knowing itself; if the colors change while you sit, name the new ones.
Cetasika. A mental factor: something that arises with each moment of consciousness and colors it. Today's word.
Your line: what colors the mind. The knowing goes on knowing; the colors keep changing. See you tomorrow.

1073.title: Seven in every moment
1073.hook: contact, feeling, perception, intention, one-pointedness, life, attention: present in every mind-moment
1073.howItsDone: Abhidhamma students learn the seven universal factors by their Pali names, and some insight meditation teachers ask students to notice contact and the tone of feeling, pleasant, unpleasant or neutral, as it arises.

segments.voice: Yesterday, cetasika, the mental factors that color each moment of knowing. Your line: what colors the mind.

A king once asked a monk to do something impossible. The king was Milinda, the monk was Nagasena, and their long conversation was written down as the Questions of King Milinda. Nagasena had been naming what happens in the mind in a single moment: contact, feeling, perception, intention, and more. So the king pushed. Can you pull them apart? Show me this one here, and that one over there. Nagasena answered him with a kitchen.
screen: `A KING AND A MONK.` → `PULL THEM APART?` → `AN ANSWER FROM THE KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: Suppose, he said, the royal cook makes a sauce with curds and salt and ginger and pepper. If the king said, bring me just the taste of the salt, could the cook do it? No. Every flavor is really there, each with its own character, but none can be lifted out alone. The Abhidhammattha Sangaha names seven mental factors present in every moment of consciousness, whatever kind it is: kind or cruel, sharp or sleepy. Contact, phassa: the mind meets its object, like two hands meeting in a clap. Feeling, vedana: that meeting has a tone, pleasant, unpleasant, or neither. Perception, sanna: the object is recognized and marked, this is blue, this is my sister's voice. Intention, cetana: the mind leans and organizes, aiming somewhere. One-pointedness: it rests on one object, even for an instant. The life faculty: what keeps the others going for as long as the moment lasts. And attention, manasikara: the mind turned toward this rather than that. Seven, in a moment of reading a street sign, a moment of anger, a moment of compassion. That's what makes the list useful. Feeling is in every moment, so no moment is without some tone. Intention is in every moment, so the mind is always leaning somewhere, even when it seems idle. And attention is always pointed, so the question is never whether the mind is attending, only to what. The sauce can't be separated in the bowl. The Abhidhamma names its parts anyway, not to take the sauce apart, but so more of it can be tasted.
screen: `THE SAUCE CAN'T BE UNMIXED.` · `SEVEN IN EVERY MOMENT.` · `ALWAYS A TONE, ALWAYS A LEAN.` · then, large: `NAMED, SO MORE CAN BE TASTED.`

segments.voice: If you'd like, rest one hand on your knee or a table and notice the moment it touches, contact, and the tone that comes with it: pleasant, unpleasant or neither. Lift it and set it down again, then try the same with a sound in the room, and with the breath at the nostrils. Just two things each time, it touched and it had a tone; the other five are there whether you find them or not.
Seven in every moment. Contact, feeling, perception, intention, one-pointedness, life and attention: the factors the manual finds in every moment of mind. Today's word.
Your line: seven always. Always a tone, always a lean, even in an idle moment. Go gently.

1074.title: The unwholesome four
1074.hook: delusion, shamelessness, recklessness, restlessness: present in every unwholesome moment
1074.howItsDone: Abhidhamma students learn the four unwholesome universals by their Pali names, and some meditation teachers in Theravada communities encourage students to notice restlessness as a sign that an unskillful state is present.

segments.voice: Yesterday, seven factors in every moment, from contact and feeling to attention. Your line: seven always.

"As rain breaks through an ill-thatched house, passion will break through an unreflecting mind." That's a verse from the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's old translation. A roof with gaps doesn't look like trouble on a dry afternoon. It shows itself when the weather turns, one drip at a time, right over the bed. Today the Abhidhamma points at the gaps: four factors it finds in every unwholesome moment of mind, whatever else is going on in it.
screen: `AN ILL-THATCHED HOUSE.` → `THE GAPS SHOW IN THE RAIN.` → `FOUR GAPS.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Unwholesome translates akusala, the opposite of kusala, skillful or healthy. It's not a verdict on a person. In the suttas, the Buddha tells his son Rahula to look at an action before, during and after it, and to ask one thing: does this lead to harm, for me, for others, or for both? A state that leads to harm is unskillful. That's the test, not a label. Now the four. The Abhidhammattha Sangaha says that whenever a moment is unwholesome, these are present. Delusion, moha: the mind can't see clearly what it's doing, like walking in fog. Shamelessness, ahirika: no inner pull of, this isn't who I want to be. Recklessness, anottappa: no care for what the act will do, to others or to oneself. And restlessness, uddhacca: the mind can't settle, like water stirred by wind. Here's something easy to miss. Greed and anger aren't on this list. They come and go, and the manual gives each its own family, coming over the next two days. These four sit underneath every unwholesome moment, a sharp word or a quiet bit of cruelty. Restlessness may be the easiest of them to feel. On this account, an unwholesome moment is never fully at rest; there's a jitter in it. So nobody has to diagnose their own heart from the inside. It's enough to feel for agitation, in the jaw, the hands, the speed of the next thought. Later this week, the manual shows the other side: two factors that are the exact opposites of shamelessness and recklessness.
screen: `UNSKILLFUL, NOT A VERDICT.` · `FOG, NO SHAME, NO CARE, NO REST.` · `GREED AND ANGER: THEIR OWN FAMILIES.` · then, large: `FEEL FOR THE JITTER.`

segments.voice: If you'd like, let the breath come and go, then feel for any restlessness at all: a foot that wants to jiggle, a mind skipping to the next thing, a pull toward the phone. Don't call it bad; just find where it lives, the hands, the chest, behind the eyes. Let one long breath out and see whether it settles a little or not; either way, it has been seen, and that is the whole practice.
The unwholesome four. Delusion, shamelessness, recklessness and restlessness: the four the manual finds in every unwholesome moment. Today's word.
Your line: the troubled four. Where the roof jitters, rain is getting in. That's today, done.

1075.title: Better, equal, worse
1075.carry: greed holds on, and conceit measures, even downward
1075.howItsDone: Abhidhamma students learn greed, wrong view and conceit as the greed-group of unwholesome factors, and some meditation teachers ask students to note 'wanting' or 'comparing' when these arise.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the unwholesome four: delusion, shamelessness, recklessness and restlessness. Your line: the troubled four.

Eleven at night. A shopping cart on a phone holds one thing, then two, then a third that was never on any list. Nothing dramatic has happened. Nobody was hurt. No rule was broken. And still the mind has been leaning forward for an hour, reaching. Today the manual introduces one of the families that grows on top of yesterday's four, and the family starts with that lean.
screen: `ELEVEN AT NIGHT.` → `ONE MORE IN THE CART.` → `THE LEAN.`

segments.voice: The head of the family is lobha, greed. In the Abhidhamma it reaches wider than wanting money. It's any holding on: to a taste, a plan, a person, the feeling of being right. The Dhammapada puts it in one line, in Max Müller's words: "There is no fire like passion, there is no shark like hatred, there is no snare like folly, there is no torrent like greed." A torrent carries things away with it. The Abhidhammattha Sangaha gives greed two relatives that appear only in its company. The first is wrong view, ditthi: a view that misreads how things are, held tight. Notice where the manual puts it: with greed, not with anger. A wrong view, on this account, is something the mind clings to, the way a hand closes around a snack. The second relative is conceit, mana. Conceit is measuring. The suttas describe it in three shapes: I'm better, I'm equal, I'm worse. All three count. Running yourself down is still measuring, still the self standing on the scale. And a fine detail: the manual says wrong view and conceit never arise in the same moment. One grips an idea; the other grips a ranking of me. So the family has three members, wanting, gripping a view, and measuring, and they can look nothing alike: a cart at eleven at night, an argument that has to be won, a quiet comparison at a reunion. The Abhidhamma's point is that they share one root, the mind leaning toward something and holding on.
screen: `GREED IS ANY HOLDING ON.` · `A VIEW CAN BE CLUNG TO.` · `BETTER, EQUAL, WORSE.` · then, large: `ONE ROOT: THE LEAN.`

segments.voice: If you'd like, bring to mind someone you saw or heard about recently, a friend, a neighbor, a stranger online, and watch for the scale: does a small voice say better, or worse, or about the same? That's conceit, the measuring; no need to argue with it, just see the scale come out and let it go back in the drawer. Then return to the breath, which isn't better or worse than anyone's.
Greed's family. Greed, wrong view and conceit: wanting, gripping a view, and measuring oneself. Today's word.
Your line: greed holds on, and conceit measures, even downward. Wanting, a view held tight, and the scale: one lean. See you tomorrow.

1076.title: Envy, stinginess and regret
1076.carry: envy pushes away; harbored thoughts keep it fed
1076.howItsDone: Abhidhamma students learn aversion, envy, stinginess and regret as the hate-group of unwholesome factors, and in some Buddhist communities people meet envy by deliberately rejoicing in others' good fortune.

segments.voice: Yesterday, greed's family: greed, wrong view and conceit. Your line: greed holds on, and conceit measures, even downward.

A text arrives from an old classmate. She got the job, the one both of them applied for. The reply goes out fast: congratulations, three exclamation points, a party emoji. And underneath the exclamation points, something small turns its face away. Yesterday's family leaned toward things. Today's family leans the other way. The Abhidhamma has a name for that turning away, and it gives it three relatives, one of which is a surprise.

The head of this family is dosa, aversion: not toward, but away. In the Abhidhamma it covers the whole range, from fury down to a mild ugh: irritation, dread, sulking, the small flinch at a voice in the next room. The Abhidhammattha Sangaha gives it three relatives that appear only in its company. Envy, issa: the mind that can't bear someone else's good fortune. Stinginess, macchariya: the mind that can't bear sharing its own. Envy watches their plate; stinginess guards mine. Both push something away, so the manual seats them with aversion, not with greed. The third relative is kukkucca, regret, or worry: brooding over a thing done that shouldn't have been, or a thing left undone that should have been. Regret can sound like conscience. But in this list, the stewing kind is a pushing against the past, aversion turned back on oneself. Seeing a mistake clearly and making amends is a different matter. What keeps this family fed? The Dhammapada answers near its start, in Max Müller's words: "'He abused me, he beat me, he defeated me, he robbed me,'--in those who harbour such thoughts hatred will never cease." Harbor is the telling word. A harbor is where boats are tied up and kept. Envy works the same way: one comparison, tied up and replayed. Regret too: one evening, docked and visited every night. In a few days this path meets the factor the tradition sets against envy, gladness at someone else's good.

If it's there, that's envy, and it's only a moment; don't scold it, just feel where it sits. Then, if you can, add one plain thought, good for them, even if it isn't fully meant, and see what happens to the tightness.

Your line: envy pushes away; harbored thoughts keep it fed. It doesn't need new reasons; it lives on the ones already kept. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1077.title: Dullness and doubt
1077.howItsDone: Some meditation teachers offer remedies for drowsiness like those given to Moggallana, such as opening the eyes, walking meditation or recalling a teaching, and Abhidhamma students learn sloth, torpor and doubt as the last of the unwholesome factors.

segments.voice: Yesterday, aversion's family: aversion, envy, stinginess and regret. Your line: aversion's family.

Moggallana was nodding off. The story is in the Anguttara Nikaya: one of the Buddha's chief disciples, sitting in meditation near a village, head drooping the way heads droop in a warm room after lunch. And the Buddha, the sutta says, came to him and didn't scold. He gave him a list of things to try. Today, the factors that drooped Moggallana's head, and one more that leaves a traveler standing at a fork in the road.
screen: `MOGGALLANA NODS OFF.` → `NO SCOLDING.` → `A LIST OF THINGS TO TRY.`

segments.voice: The Abhidhammattha Sangaha names two factors that travel together: thina and middha, usually put into English as sloth and torpor. Sloth is sluggishness of mind, thinking through syrup. Torpor is the heaviness, the drowse, the eyelids. Neither one is rest. Rest is chosen and it restores; this is the mind going dim while it's trying to stay awake. The suttas count the pair as one of the five hindrances, and in the Digha Nikaya each hindrance gets a picture. Being free of sloth and torpor is like being let out of prison. Doubt, vicikiccha, gets its own picture: being free of it is like reaching safety after a dangerous road through a desert. This doubt isn't a good question; questions get asked and answered. It's the mind at a fork, never choosing, sitting down in the sand. Now, the list the Buddha gave Moggallana. Change the thought you were on when the drowsiness came. Recall a teaching, or recite it aloud. Pull your earlobes and rub your arms. Get up, splash water on your eyes, look out at the sky and the stars. Hold the perception of light, as bright by night as by day. Walk up and down. And if none of that works, lie down, mindfully, intending to get up. It's a practical list, with no shame anywhere in it, and its last resort is simply sleep. For doubt, the suttas name a different remedy: careful attention to what is skillful and what isn't, looked at again and again, until the fork resolves. A mind at a crossroads doesn't need more roads to consider. It needs one step.

1078.title: The beautiful factors
1078.hook: faith, mindfulness, conscience, concern, non-greed, non-hate, balance
1078.howItsDone: Abhidhamma students learn the beautiful factors by their Pali names alongside the unwholesome ones, and some Theravada teachers call hiri and ottappa, conscience and concern, the guardians of the world.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dullness and doubt: sloth, torpor, and a mind stuck at a fork. Your line: dull and doubtful.

The manual could have called them the good factors. It calls them the beautiful ones, sobhana. All week this path has been naming what troubles a moment of mind: the four under every unwholesome moment, greed's family, aversion's family, dullness and doubt. A long list, and an honest one. Today the week closes by turning the cloth over, and the manual's other side begins with seven.
screen: `NOT GOOD: BEAUTIFUL.` → `A WEEK OF TROUBLES.` → `TURN THE CLOTH OVER.`

segments.voice: First, faith, saddha. In the Questions of King Milinda, Nagasena gives faith a picture. A king's army crosses a stream and churns it to mud. The king is thirsty. A water-clearing gem is dropped in, the mud settles, and the water is fit to drink. Faith, in that picture, is less about believing hard and more about the mind settling clear. Second, mindfulness, sati: the mind that doesn't float off, that stays with what's here. Third and fourth come as a pair. Conscience, hiri: the inner pull of, this is beneath me. Concern, ottappa: care for what an act will do. The troubled four included shamelessness and recklessness; these are their exact opposites. In the Anguttara Nikaya, the Buddha calls this pair two bright qualities that protect the world. Then non-greed, alobha: the open hand. Non-hate, adosa: the friendly face that doesn't turn away. And balance, tatramajjhattata: evenness, a mind holding things without tipping. These seven, with tomorrow's six pairs, the manual finds in every beautiful moment of mind. They aren't rare peak experiences: a settled mind, a mind that stays, some self-respect, some care, an open hand, a friendly face, an even keel. The Dhammapada sums up the teaching in one verse, in Max Müller's words: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened." The beautiful factors are what that purifying looks like from inside, one moment at a time. A moment can be colored by greed, envy, fog, or by faith, care and an open hand. The same knowing, a different dye.
screen: `FAITH CLEARS THE WATER.` · `CONSCIENCE AND CONCERN GUARD.` · `AN OPEN HAND, A FRIENDLY FACE.` · then, large: `SAME KNOWING, DIFFERENT DYE.`

segments.voice: If you'd like, look for something beautiful in this moment, in the manual's sense: mindfulness, the mind staying with the breath; balance, a little evenness; or non-hate, someone comes to mind and the face doesn't turn away. Find one and name it quietly, the way the troubled ones were named all week. Let it be as small as it is; small still counts.
Sobhana. Beautiful: the manual's name for the factors that color a moment well. Today's word.
Your line: the beautiful. Faith, care and an open hand, each one a moment. A week of factors, done.
